origin_region: Valle del Cauca · La Cumbre · Bitaco
cultivar: Sinensis and assamica cultivars, the first plants reportedly from Sri Lanka, planted from the 1950s onwards
processing: Orthodox tea from a single high-altitude estate: leaf withered, rolled, fully oxidised and fired. The estate gave up CTC around 2016; it also makes green, white, a little oolong and roasted green tea, the specialty line being certified organic.
harvest_season: Plucked all year on the equator, on a cycle of a few weeks; the drier months (roughly December to March and July to August) give the brightest leaf, but there are no seasonal grades.
appearance_dry: Dark, wiry, twisted leaves with a few golden tips in the specialty grade; small broken leaf in the tea-bag grade.
taste_profile: Mild, soft and lightly floral with a gentle malt, a honeyed sweetness and low tannin; a clean, easy high-grown black tea that sits between a light Ceylon and a Darjeeling second flush in weight.

brewing.notes: Western style, three minutes, no milk needed; the whole-leaf specialty grade can be steeped shorter and resteeped once or twice.

vintage_note: Sold year-round under the estate's domestic brand (Hindú) in tea bags across Colombia, and as 'Bitaco' specialty loose leaf in small packs from the estate and a few export partners; neither is dated by harvest, since the equatorial estate picks continuously. Buy the loose specialty grade and use it within a year or two.
description:
Colombia is coffee country, and its one tea estate is a curiosity most Colombians have never heard of, even though many of them drink its tea. Bitaco is a plantation in the cloud forest above La Cumbre in Valle del Cauca, at around 1,800 to 2,050 metres, owned by Agrícola Himalaya, the company behind the Hindú tea-bag brand that sits on supermarket shelves across the country. The gardens were planted from the 1950s, the first plants reportedly of Sri Lankan origin, and have been expanded and modernised since.

The estate makes orthodox black tea, plus green, white and a little oolong, in its own factory; it made CTC too until around 2016. The Hindú brand is the mass-market line; a specialty line, organic and sold under the Bitaco name, is where the whole-leaf teas end up, and it is this line that has reached specialty shops abroad over the last decade.

The black tea is high-grown and tastes it: mild, soft and lightly floral, with gentle malt, honeyed sweetness and low tannin, nearer to a light Ceylon or a Darjeeling second flush than to anything heavy. It is clean and easy, brews well Western-style without milk, and the whole-leaf grade takes a second steep. It is not a tea of great depth, but it is a well-made one from a place nobody expects.

In Colombia you will meet it as Hindú tea bags; the thing to buy is the Bitaco loose leaf, from the estate's shop, Colombian specialty retailers or the few importers who carry it. There are no fakes and no vintages, only the choice between the bag grade and the specialty grade.

If you collect single-estate teas from unexpected places, Bitaco belongs on the shelf beside Gorreana from the Azores and Charleston from South Carolina; and the natural comparison in the cup is a mid-grown Ceylon.
history:
Colombian tea begins with a farm policy: in 1946 the agriculture office of Valle del Cauca brought in tea plants, reportedly the first from Sri Lanka. In the 1950s Joaquín Llano González and his son Alberto Llano Buenaventura became the first commercial growers, at their farms in Bitaco. Alberto studied tea processing in Peru, made his first finished tea in 1954 and sold it as Té La Sofía; the Hindú brand of broken-leaf tea bags followed in 1960.

After his death in 1982 the family re-formed the business as Agrícola Himalaya in 1984, and Hindú became the leading tea brand in Colombia. Later came UTZ certification in 2011, a turn to organic, fine-plucked tea under the Bitaco name from 2013, and an end to CTC at the estate around 2016.

The farm is small, about 62 hectares at 1,800 to 2,050 metres, and black loose leaf is the bulk of what it makes.
